latin_text: CAP. II. De duodecim Philippi discipulis, et Josepho Arimathæensi, Glastoniensium monachorum traditiones; veterum nominibus fucatæ, et in Europæorum generalibus conciliis venditatæ.

translation_history.english: CHAPTER II. The traditions of the monks of Glastonbury concerning the twelve disciples of Philip and Joseph of Arimathea; disguised under the names of the ancients, and paraded about in the general councils of the European nations.

latin_text: AD Glastoniensium monachorum, de Josepho Arimathæensi et ejus sociis, traditiones nunc venio: quas etsi Normannorum adventu antiquiores non existimem, et posteriorum temporum superstitionem plane redoleant; tamen qualescunque sunt, ex Guilielmi Malmesburiensis de antiquitate Glastoniensis ecclesiæ libello exhibere visum est.

translation_history.english: I now come to the traditions of the monks of Glastonbury concerning Joseph of Arimathea and his companions: and although I do not think them older than the coming of the Normans, and they plainly smack of the superstition of later ages, yet, such as they are, I have seen fit to present them from the little treatise of William of Malmesbury on the antiquity of the church of Glastonbury.

latin_text: Sic igitur ille, præmissa præfatione ad Henricum Blesensem, Henrici I. regis ex Adela sorore nepotem, Wintoniensem tum episcopum et Glastoniensem abbatem, archæologiam suam ab apostolicis exorditur temporibus.

translation_history.english: And so, having prefaced a preface addressed to Henry of Blois — nephew of King Henry I through his sister Adela, at that time bishop of Winchester and abbot of Glastonbury — he begins his antiquarian account from apostolic times.

latin_text: " Post Dominicæ resurrectionis gloriam, ascensionisque triumphum, ac Spiritus paracliti de supernis missionem (qui discipulorum corda temporalis pœnæ adhuc formidine trepidantia replevit, scientiam omnium linguarum tribuendo) erant omnes credentes simul cum mulieribus, et Maria matre Jesu, ut Lucas narrat evangelista: et verbum Dei disseminabatur, crescebatque numerus credentium quotidie; eratque omnibus cor unum et anima una. Invidiæ ergo facibus accensi sacerdotes Judæorum cum Pharisæis et Scribis, concitaverunt persecutionem in Ecclesia, interficiendo protomartyrem Stephanum, et fere a finibus suis omnes procul pellentes. Hac igitur persecutionis procella sæviente, dispersi credentes petierunt diversa regna terrarum a Domino sibi delegata, verbum salutis gentibus propinando. Sanctus autem Philippus, ut testatur Freculphus libro secundo, capitulo quarto, regionem Francorum adiens gratia prædicandi plures ad fidem convertit et baptizavit. Volens igitur verbum Christi dilatari, duodecim ex suis discipulis elegit, et ad evangelizandum verbum vitæ misit in Britanniam: quibus, ut ferunt, charissimum amicum suum Joseph ab Arimathia, qui et Dominum sepelivit, præfecit. Venientes igitur in Britanniam anno ab incarnatione Domini sexagesimo tertio, ab assumptione beatæ Mariæ decimoquinto, fidem Christi fiducialiter prædicabant. Rex autem barbarus cum sua gente, tam nova audiens et inconsueta, omnino prædicationi eorum consentire renuebat, nec paternas traditiones commutare volebat: quia tamen de longe venerant, vitæque eorum exigebat modestia; quandam insulam sylvis, rubis atque paludibus circundatam, ab incolis Ynswitrin nuncupatam, in lateribus suæ regionis ad habitandum concessit.

translation_history.english: "After the glory of the Lord's resurrection and the triumph of his ascension, and the sending of the Paraclete Spirit from on high (who filled the hearts of the disciples, still trembling with dread of temporal punishment, by bestowing on them the knowledge of all tongues), all the believers were together with the women, and with Mary the mother of Jesus, as Luke the evangelist relates: and the word of God was being spread abroad, and the number of believers grew daily; and they all had one heart and one soul. Then the priests of the Jews, kindled with the torches of envy, together with the Pharisees and Scribes, stirred up a persecution against the Church, putting to death the protomartyr Stephen and driving almost all the believers far off from their borders. And so, while this storm of persecution raged, the scattered believers sought out the various kingdoms of the earth allotted to them by the Lord, offering the word of salvation to the peoples. Now Saint Philip, as Freculph testifies in book two, chapter four, went into the region of the Franks and converted many to the faith and baptized them. Wishing therefore that the word of Christ should be spread more widely, he chose twelve of his disciples and sent them into Britain to evangelize the word of life; over them, as they report, he set his dearest friend Joseph of Arimathea, who had also buried the Lord. Coming therefore into Britain in the sixty-third year from the incarnation of the Lord, and the fifteenth from the assumption of the blessed Mary, they preached the faith of Christ with confidence. But the barbarian king, together with his people, hearing things so new and unaccustomed, refused altogether to consent to their preaching, and was unwilling to change his ancestral traditions: yet, because they had come from afar, and the modesty of their life demanded it, he granted them a certain island, surrounded by woods, brambles, and marshes, called by the inhabitants Ynswitrin, on the borders of his territory, to dwell in."

latin_text: Postea etiam alii duo reges pagani successive comperta vitæ eorum sanctimonia, unicuique eorum unam portionem terræ concesserunt; ac ad petitionem ipsorum, secundum morem gentis, brevi^a dictas duodecim hidas confirmaverunt. Unde et duodecim hidæ per eos adhuc, ut creditur, nomen sortiuntur."

translation_history.english: Afterwards two other pagan kings also, one after the other, having learned of the holiness of their life, each granted them one portion of land; and at their request, according to the custom of the people, they confirmed the said twelve hides by charter.^a Hence it is believed that the twelve hides still take their name from them."

latin_text: " Prædicti itaque sancti in eodem deserto conversantes, post pusillum temporis visione archangeli Gabrielis admoniti sunt ecclesiam in honore sanctæ Dei genitricis et virginis Mariæ, in loco cœlitus eis demonstrato construere.

translation_history.english: " The aforesaid saints, then, living in that same wilderness, were after a short time admonished by a vision of the archangel Gabriel to build a church in honour of the holy Mother of God and Virgin Mary, in a place shown to them from heaven.

latin_text: Qui divinis præceptis non segniter obedientes, secundum quod eis fuerat ostensum, quandam capellam, inferius per circuitum virgis torquatis muros perficientes, consummaverunt in anno post passionem Domini tricesimo primo, post assumptionem gloriosæ virginis decimo quinto, et deformi quidem schemate, sed Dei multipliciter adornatam virtute. Et cum hæc in hac regione prima fuerit; ampliori eam dignitate Dei filius insignivit, ipsam videlicet in honore suæ matris dedicando. Duodecim igitur sancti sæpius memorati, in eodem loco Deo et beatæ virgini devota exhibentes obsequia; vigiliis, jejuniis et orationibus vacantes, ejusdem virginis auxilio ac visione (ut credi pium est) in omnibus necessitatibus refocillabantur. Hæc autem ita se habere, tum ex charta beati Patricii, tum ex scriptis seniorum cognoscimus.”

translation_history.english: Obeying the divine commands without delay, they completed, in accordance with what had been shown to them, a certain chapel, finishing its walls below with twisted wattles all around, in the thirty-first year after the Lord's passion and the fifteenth after the assumption of the glorious Virgin; of unshapely form, indeed, but richly adorned by the power of God. And since this was the first in this region, the Son of God distinguished it with a greater dignity, namely by dedicating it in honour of his mother. The twelve saints so often mentioned, therefore, offering devout service to God and the blessed Virgin in that same place, and giving themselves to vigils, fasts, and prayers, were sustained in all their needs by the aid and the vision of that same Virgin (as it is pious to believe). That these things are so, I know both from the charter of the blessed Patrick and from the writings of the elders.”

latin_text: Literis.

translation_history.english: ^a “By letters” (literis): a variant reading for brevi, “by charter.”

latin_text: Addit præterea Malmesburiensis, ad Glastoniensis ecclesiæ antiquitatem comprobandam, et sequens testimonium: “Monachus quidam Glastoniæ, Godefridus nomine, (de cujus epistola hoc capitulum assumpsimus) tempore Henrici Blesensis, abbatis Glastoniensis, cum in pago Parisiacensi apud sanctum Dionysium moraretur; senior quidam ex monachis interrogavit eum: quo genus, unde domo? Respondit, Normannum, e Britanniæ monasterio quod Glastingeia dicitur, monachum. Papæ, inquit, an adhuc stat illa perpetuæ virginis et misericordiæ matris vetusta ecclesia? Stat, inquit. Tum ille lepido attactu caput G. Glastoniensis demulcens, diu silentio suspensum tenuit, ac sic demum ora resolvit; hæc gloriosissimi martyris Dionysii ecclesia, et illa de qua te asseris, eandem privilegii dignitatem habent: ista in Gallia, illa in Britannia uno eodem tempore exortæ, a summo et magno pontifice consecratæ. Uno tamen gradu illa supereminet: Roma etenim secunda vocatur.”

translation_history.english: William of Malmesbury adds besides, in confirmation of the antiquity of the church of Glastonbury, the following testimony as well: “A certain monk of Glastonbury named Godfrey (from whose letter I have taken this chapter), while he was staying at Saint-Denis in the district of Paris in the time of Henry of Blois, abbot of Glastonbury, was questioned by one of the older monks: of what family, and from what house? He answered that he was a Norman, a monk from a monastery in Britain called Glastingeia. ‘Good heavens,’ said the old man, ‘does that ancient church of the perpetual Virgin and mother of mercy still stand?’ ‘It stands,’ he replied. Then the old man, stroking the head of G. of Glastonbury with a kindly touch, held him a long while in suspense in silence, and at last opened his lips thus: this church of the most glorious martyr Denis, and that one to which you say you belong, have one and the same dignity of privilege: the one arose in Gaul, the other in Britain, at one and the same time, and both were consecrated by the supreme and great pontiff. In one degree, however, yours stands higher: for it is called a second Rome.”

latin_text: Refert Cæsar Baronius ex^b actis Mariæ Magdalenæ et sociorum, dispersione facta post mortem Stephani, “Lazarum, Mariam Magdalenam, Martham, et Marcellam pedissequam, in quos Judæi majori odio exardescebant, non tantum Hierosolymis pulsos esse, sed una cum Maximino discipulo, navi absque remigio impositos, in certum periculum mari fuisse creditos: quos divina providentia Massiliam tradunt appulisse.” Additque ex historia Anglorum, quæ manuscripta habetur in bibliotheca Vaticana, sed (quod ille tacet, et nos suo loco patefaciemus) nostris temporibus scripta, “comitem ejusdem discriminis Josephum ab Arimathæa nobilem decurionem; quem tradunt ex Gallia in Britanniam navigasse, illicque post prædicatum evangelium diem clausisse extremum.” In PseudoDextri quoque chronico, ad annum Christi XLVIII. similiter legimus; “ Hierosolymitani Judæi vehementer infensi B. Lazaro, Magdalenæ, Marthæ, Marcellæ, Maximino, Josepho ab Arimathia nobili decurioni, et aliis plurimis ; navi sine remigio velisque, ac sine gubernatore eos imponunt, et exulare mandant : qui per vastum mare divinitus delati, ad Massiliensem portum incolumes appellunt.” Et in fragmento Helecæ attributo; “Fama est, Magdalenam Lazari sororem, cum Lazaro, Maximo atque Chelidonio, Marcella, Josepho ab Arimathia, venisse in Galliam Aquitanicam; ibique prædicasse Domini Jesu sanctum evangelium: ut docent luculenter Gallorum historiæ, et est traditio ubique satis recepta illius regionis.” Quod autem de Philippi in Galliis apostolatu habet Freculphus a Malmesburiensi citatus; ex Isidori libro de patribus utriusque Testamenti^c ad verbum expressit. Apud utrumque enim legimus, Philippum Gallis prædicasse Christum, “ barbarasque gentes, vicinasque tenebris, et tumenti oceano conjunctas, ad scientiæ lucem, fideique portum deduxisse.” Neque hic mihi Baronii^d conjectura placet, Isidori ista a Gallis nostris ad Galatas Asiaticos traducentis : multoque minus, nuperi operum Isidori editoris, Jacobi Breulii temeritas, Galatis pro Gallis in ipso textu, sine ulla veteris lectionis commemoratione, reponentis.

translation_history.english: Cesare Baronius reports, from^b the acts of Mary Magdalene and her companions, that when the dispersion took place after the death of Stephen, “Lazarus, Mary Magdalene, Martha, and Marcella her attendant, against whom the Jews blazed with the fiercer hatred, were not only driven out of Jerusalem but, together with the disciple Maximinus, were put aboard a ship without oars and committed to the sea to certain peril; and these, they relate, divine providence brought safely to Marseilles.” And he adds, from a history of the English which is kept in manuscript in the Vatican Library but (a point he passes over in silence, and which I will disclose in its proper place) was written in our own times, that “a companion in the same danger was Joseph of Arimathea, the noble decurion; who, they relate, sailed from Gaul into Britain, and there, after preaching the gospel, ended his last day.” In the chronicle of Pseudo-Dexter too, at the year of Christ 48, I read much the same: “The Jews of Jerusalem, violently hostile to the blessed Lazarus, Magdalene, Martha, Marcella, Maximinus, Joseph of Arimathea the noble decurion, and very many others, put them aboard a ship without oars or sails and without a helmsman, and order them into exile; and they, carried across the open sea by divine guidance, come safely to port at Marseilles.” And in the fragment attributed to Heleca: “The report is that Magdalene, the sister of Lazarus, came with Lazarus, Maximus, and Chelidonius, with Marcella and Joseph of Arimathea, into Aquitanian Gaul, and there preached the holy gospel of the Lord Jesus, as the histories of the Gauls plainly teach, and as is a tradition well enough received everywhere in that region.” As for what Freculph, cited by William of Malmesbury, has to say about Philip’s apostolate in the Gauls, he took it word for word from Isidore’s book “On the Fathers of Both Testaments”^c. For in both authors I read that Philip preached Christ to the Gauls, and “led barbarous peoples, bordering upon darkness and joined to the swelling ocean, to the light of knowledge and the harbour of faith.” Nor am I satisfied here with the conjecture of Baronius^d, who transfers these words of Isidore from our Gauls to the Galatians of Asia; and still less with the rashness of Jacques du Breul, the recent editor of Isidore’s works, who puts “Galatians” for “Gauls” in the text itself, without any notice whatever of the older reading.

latin_text: Baron. annal. tom. 1. ann. 35. sec. 5. Vid. Petrum de Natalibus, lib. 6. cap. 124. Melchiorem Inchofer, de veritate epistolæ B. Mariæ ad Messanenses, cap. 13. et Fran. Bosquet. eccles. Gallican. hist. lib. 1. sec. 3.

translation_history.english: ^b Baronius, Annals, vol. 1, year 35, sec. 5. See Pietro de’ Natali, book 6, chapter 124; Melchior Inchofer, “On the Authenticity of the Letter of the Blessed Virgin Mary to the People of Messina”, chapter 13; and François Bosquet, “Ecclesiastical History of the Gauls”, book 1, sec. 3.

latin_text: Nam præterquam quod Isidorus in hoc ipso opere, capite secundo et octogesimo et in officio Toletano, quod^e Gothicum et Mozarabum vulgo appellatur : itemque Julianus Toletanus archiepiscopus in Nahum^f prophetam scribens, et Beda (vel quicunque author fuit collectaneorum et florum ad calcem tertii tomi operum ipsius adjectorum) Philippo Galliam assignant: idemque “ Gallis prædicavisse Christum” legitur, in libello de festis apostolorum, qui in Hieronymiano martyrologio manuscripto habetur, ex quo pleraque omnia in librum suum de patribus novi Testamenti transcripsit Isidorus: illa barbararum gentium oceano conjunctarum mentio, Europæos Gallos, non GalloGræcos ab Isidoro intellectos esse satis evincit.

translation_history.english: For quite apart from the fact that Isidore, in this very work, at chapter 82, and in the Toledan office, which^e is commonly called the Gothic or Mozarabic, and likewise Julian, archbishop of Toledo, writing on the prophet Nahum,^f and Bede (or whoever the author was of the collectanea and florilegia appended at the end of the third volume of his works) all assign Gaul to Philip — and apart from the fact that the same thing, that he “preached Christ to the Gauls,” is read in the little book on the feasts of the apostles contained in the manuscript Hieronymian martyrology, from which Isidore transcribed almost everything into his own book on the fathers of the New Testament — that mention of barbarous peoples bordering on the ocean is enough to prove that Isidore understood the Gauls of Europe, not the Gallo-Greeks.

latin_text: Vid. cap. 74.

translation_history.english: See chapter 74.

latin_text: Baron. tom. 1. ann. 44. sec. 32. et eum secutus Jacobus Valdesius, de dignitate reg. Hisp. cap. 6. sec. 56.

translation_history.english: Baronius, volume 1, year 44, section 32; and, following him, Jacobus Valdesius, "On the Dignity of the Kings of Spain," chapter 6, section 56.

latin_text: Offic. Mozar. in festo S. Jac. tomo 2. Auctarii bibliothecæ patrum, edit. Paris. ann. 1610. col. 1659. in Hymno de S. Jacobo quem inde desumptum commentario suo in Dextri chronicon inseruit Franc Bivarius, pag. 86.

translation_history.english: Mozarabic Office, on the feast of St. James, in volume 2 of the Auctarium of the Bibliotheca Patrum, Paris edition of 1610, column 1659; in the hymn on St. James which Francisco Bivar took from that source and inserted in his commentary on the Chronicle of Dexter, page 86.

latin_text: Ibid. col. 205.

translation_history.english: Ibid., column 205.

latin_text: Quod vero Josephi Arimathæensis opera in gentibus Britannicis ad fidem perducendis Philippus usus fuerit, id totum ex Glastoniensium monachorum lacunis haustum est: a quibus et barbari illi manarunt versiculi, ex chronicis quibusdam de rege Arvirago agentibus citati^g: Intrat Avalloniam duodena caterva virorum; Flos Arimathææ Joseph est primus eorum.

translation_history.english: But the notion that Philip employed the services of Joseph of Arimathea in bringing the British peoples to the faith has been drawn entirely from the cisterns of the Glastonbury monks; and from them too flowed those barbarous little verses, cited^g from certain chronicles that treat of king Arviragus: "A company of twelve men enters Avalon; Joseph, the flower of Arimathea, is the first of them."

latin_text: Josephes ex Joseph genitus patrem comitatur; His aliisque decem jus Glastoniæ propriatur.

translation_history.english: "Josephes, begotten of Joseph, accompanies his father; to these and to ten others the title to Glastonbury is made over."

latin_text: Atque ex^h aliis, paris elegantiæ, isti: Joseph cum sociis jussit transire Philippus Ad terram Britonum divinum promere verbum.

translation_history.english: And from^h others, of equal elegance, come these: "Philip bade Joseph and his companions cross over to the land of the Britons to set forth the divine word."

latin_text: Fert^i hos camisia qui promissum tenuerunt: Navigio ceteri terræ mox applicuerunt.

translation_history.english: "A shirt^i carries those who kept the promise; the rest soon reached land by ship."

latin_text: Regi consuluit Joseph tunc credere Christum: Arviragus renuit rex hoc, nec credit in ipsum.

translation_history.english: "Joseph then urged the king to believe in Christ; King Arviragus refused this, and does not believe in him."

latin_text: Glastoniæ bis sex hidas dedit Arviragus rex: Joseph cum sociis jura reliquit eis.

translation_history.english: "King Arviragus gave twelve hides at Glastonbury; Joseph with his companions left them their rights."

latin_text: Anno trigeno primo post vulnera Christi, Ecclesiam virgis faciunt cum laudibus isti.

translation_history.english: "In the thirty-first year after the wounds of Christ, these men with praises build a church of wattles."

latin_text: Habetur et hodie Welliæ in ædibus D. Thomæ Hugonis equitis aurati, tabula ænea, columnæ Glastoniensis ecclesiæ olim affixa: cui incisum legitur: “ Anno post passionem Domini XXXI. duodecim sancti, ex quibus Joseph ab Arimathia primus erat, huc venerunt, qui Ecclesiam hujus regni primam in hoc loco construxerunt, quam Christus in honorem suæ matris et locum pro eorum sepultura præsentialiter dedicavit.” Est etiam penes nobilissimum virum, D. Guilielmum Howardum, Thomæ Norfolciæ Ducis filium, ingens tabula, Glastonienses antiquitates undique conquisitas complectens : in qua, inter alia fabulosissima, et ista legimus : “ Joseph ab Arimathia beati Philippi apostoli discipulatui se contulit, atque ejus salubri doctrina aﬄuenter refertus et ab ipso cum filio suo Josepho baptizatus est. Postea vero a beato Johanne apostolo ipsi prædicationi Ephesiorum insudante, beatæ perpetuæque virginis Mariæ paranymphus delegatus est : ejusdem quoque gloriosæ virginis venerandæ assumptioni cum beato Philippo cæterisque discipulis interfuit, atque ea quæ de Domino Jesu Christo atque ejus gloriosa genitrice Maria audierat et viderat instanter per diversas regiones prædicans, ac multos convertens et baptizans ; tandem decimo quinto post eandem gloriosam assumptionem anno, cum memorato filio suo Josepho ad sanctum Philippum in Gallias venit. Ac deinde secundum quod legitur in libro qui dicitur Graal, Joseph ab Arimathia, qui dominum sepelivit, baptizatus a beato Philippo apostolo venit in majorem Britanniam, sibi et semini ejus promissam, cum uxore, et filio Josephe nomine, quem ipse Salvator noster in civitate Saraz prius in episcopum consecraverat.”

translation_history.english: There is still today at Wells, in the house of Sir Thomas Hughes, knight, a bronze tablet once affixed to a pillar of the church of Glastonbury, on which this is engraved: "In the thirty-first year after the passion of the Lord twelve holy men, of whom Joseph of Arimathea was the first, came here, and built in this place the first church of this kingdom, which Christ dedicated in person in honour of his mother and as a place for their burial." There is also in the keeping of that most noble man, Sir William Howard, son of Thomas, Duke of Norfolk, an immense tablet comprising Glastonbury antiquities collected from every quarter, in which, among other wholly fabulous matters, I read this as well: "Joseph of Arimathea gave himself to the discipleship of the blessed apostle Philip, and, abundantly filled with his wholesome doctrine, was baptized by him together with his son Josephes. Afterwards, when the blessed apostle John was labouring at the preaching to the Ephesians, Joseph was appointed guardian of the blessed and ever-virgin Mary; he was also present with the blessed Philip and the other disciples at the venerable assumption of that same glorious virgin, and, preaching earnestly through various regions the things he had heard and seen concerning the Lord Jesus Christ and his glorious mother Mary, and converting and baptizing many, he came at length, in the fifteenth year after that same glorious assumption, with his aforementioned son Josephes to Saint Philip in Gaul. And thereafter, according to what is read in the book called the Graal, Joseph of Arimathea, who buried the Lord, baptized by the blessed apostle Philip, came into greater Britain, promised to him and to his seed, with his wife and with his son named Josephes, whom our Saviour himself had previously consecrated bishop in the city of Saraz."

latin_text: Joh. Capgrav. in vita Josephi. Tabula magna Glastoniensis.

translation_history.english: ^g John Capgrave, in the Life of Joseph. The great Glastonbury tablet.

latin_text: Ex appendice chronici Glastoniensis, MS. in bibliotheca Cottoniana.

translation_history.english: ^h From the appendix to the Glastonbury chronicle, a manuscript in the Cottonian library.

latin_text: Habetur ineptissima hæc fabella in magna Glastoniensis ecclesiæ tabula, et apud Capgravium in vita Josephi.

translation_history.english: ^i This most absurd little fable is found on the great tablet of the church of Glastonbury, and in Capgrave, in the Life of Joseph.

latin_text: Sequuntur deinde portenta illa, quæ in vita Josephi refert Capgravius ex eodem nugacissimo libro, qui sanctum Graal appellatur, cujus auctor Guilielmo Malmesburiensi paulo videtur fuisse posterior ; licet ab Helinando Cluniacensi, Frigidi montis in Gallia monacho, ad annum salutis DCCXX. referatur. Sic enim ille in chronico, a Vincentio^k Bellovacensi citato : “ Hoc,” inquit, “ tempore in Britannia cuidam eremitæ monstrata est mirabilis quædam visio per angelum, de sancto Joseph decurione nobili, qui corpus Domini deposuit de cruce, et de catino illo vel de paropside, in quo Dominus cœnavit cum discipulis suis, de quo ab eodem eremita descripta est historia, quæ dicitur de Gradali. Gradalis autem vel Gradale Gallice dicitur scutella lata, et aliquantulum profunda, in qua pretiosæ dapes cum suo jure divitibus solent apponi, gradatim unus morsellus post alium in diversis ordinibus; et dicitur vulgari nomine Graal, quia grata et acceptabilis est, in ea comedenti, tum propter continens, quia forte argentea est, vel de alia pretiosa materia; tum propter contentum, id est, ordinem multiplicem dapum pretiosarum. Hanc hiſtoriam Latine scriptam inveniri non potui: sed tantum Gallice scripta habetur a quibusdam proceribus, nec facile (ut aiunt) inveniri potest.”

translation_history.english: Then follow those prodigies which Capgrave recounts in his life of Joseph out of that same most frivolous book which is called the Holy Grail, whose author appears to have lived a little later than William of Malmesbury — though Helinand of Cluny, a monk of Froidmont in France, assigns it to the year of salvation 720. For thus he writes in his chronicle, as cited by Vincent^k of Beauvais: "At this time," he says, "a certain marvellous vision was shown by an angel to a hermit in Britain, concerning the holy Joseph, the noble decurion who took down the body of the Lord from the cross, and concerning that bowl or platter in which the Lord supped with his disciples; and the hermit wrote a history of it, which is called the history of the Gradal. Now gradalis or gradale is the French word for a broad and somewhat deep dish, in which costly delicacies with their sauce are customarily set before the rich, one morsel after another by degrees in successive courses; and it is called by the common name Graal, because it is pleasing (grata) and acceptable to the one eating from it, both on account of the container, since it is perhaps of silver or of some other precious material, and on account of the contents, that is, the manifold array of costly dishes. I have not been able to find this history written in Latin: it is only to be had written in French, in the hands of certain noblemen, and (so they say) it cannot easily be found."

Fuit namque hic sapiens rex imbutus divinitus secretiore sapientia: incantationes^o composuit, quibus morbi pellerentur, et dæmones fugarentur, non redituri.”

translation_history.english: Thomas Malory transferred much from that source into the legendary deeds of King Arthur, which he published in the English language: he uses the word "Sangreal" here in a sense approaching closely the notion of "real blood," for he imagines that a portion^l of the most precious blood of our Saviour was deposited here — whether blood shed upon the cross, or blood preserved from Christ's last supper; concerning which Stephanus Forcatulus writes: "The Britons^m relate that Joseph brought with him a pledge and testimony of that sacred supper, namely the dish set before those most holy guests, which was kept for a very long time with great ceremony as a kind of pledge of British security, exactly as the Trojans kept the Palladium." So he writes; and afterwards he adds, concerning the ancient British magic supposedly augmented by Joseph, a pronouncement no less removed from reason than from religion: "Joseph of Arimathea, a newcomer whom Britain welcomed, increased^n its prodigious rites; he had drawn his art from Solomon's fountain. For that wise king had been divinely imbued with a more hidden wisdom: he composed incantations^o by which diseases were driven off and demons put to flight, never to return."

Quibus rex Arviragus, licet paganus, ne ulterius laborarent, duodecim hidas terræ eis contulit in insula Avalloniæ, quæ nunc dicitur Glastonia. In quo loco ecclesiam in honore beatæ virginis per admonitionem S. Michaelis archangeli, de virgis torquatis muros facientes, construxerunt."

translation_history.english: Concerning the twelve disciples sent into Britain by the blessed Philip, a certain monk of Malmesbury records the following in the second book of his "Eulogium": "In the year of the Lord's Incarnation 63, and the fifteenth year from the assumption of the blessed Virgin Mary, twelve disciples came into Greater Britain, sent by the blessed apostle Philip to preach the word of God there; the first of them was Joseph of Arimathea, who buried Jesus Christ. King Arviragus, though a pagan, granted them twelve hides of land in the island of Avalon, now called Glastonbury, so that they should labour no further. In that place, at the admonition of St Michael the archangel, they built a church in honour of the blessed Virgin, making its walls of twisted wattles."

Mariæ fuit constructum, in anno post assumptionem ejusdem quinto decimo." Et in ali0^q, a monacho cœnobii S. Augustini Cantuariensis anno MCCCCVI. conscripto: "Rex Yna fuit primus fundator monasterii Glastoniensis. Monachi tamen ibidem aliam prætendunt fundationem a rege Arvirago (filio Kimbelini regis Britonum, in cujus tempore Christus Jesus de Maria virgine natus fuit) et quod ab Arthuro rege dotatum fuit pluribus possessionibus." Item in libro de prærogativis et dignitatibus ordinem monasticum concernentibus, qui a Thoma Walsinghamio scriptus putatur: "S. Philippus apostolus Jesu Christi misit in Britanniam duodecim prædicatores, quorum primus et præcipuus fuit Joseph ab Arimathia, qui Christum sepelivit. Qui Glasconiam venientes, acceperunt possessionem hidarum duodecim, ab Arvirago nobili rege Britanniæ, adhuc paganicis erroribus involuto. Hi per Gabrielis archangeli admonitionem, ecclesiam in honore sanctæ Dei genetricis Mariæ construxerunt anno post passionem Domini tricesimo primo."

translation_history.english: In a Glastonbury chronicle^p likewise, drawn up in the year 1259, I read the following written: "In the year 63 from the Incarnation, disciples of the holy apostles Philip and James came into Britain; by them the first oratory on the island of Avalon was built in honour of St. Mary, in the fifteenth year after her assumption." And in another^q, composed by a monk of the monastery of St. Augustine at Canterbury in the year 1406: "King Ina was the first founder of the monastery of Glastonbury. The monks there, however, allege another foundation, by king Arviragus (son of Kimbelinus king of the Britons, in whose time Christ Jesus was born of the Virgin Mary), and that it was endowed by king Arthur with many possessions." Likewise in the book on the prerogatives and dignities pertaining to the monastic order, which is thought to have been written by Thomas Walsingham: "St. Philip, apostle of Jesus Christ, sent twelve preachers into Britain, of whom the first and chief was Joseph of Arimathea, who buried Christ. Coming to Glastonbury, they received a holding of twelve hides from Arviragus, a noble king of Britain, who was still entangled in pagan errors. These men, at the admonition of the archangel Gabriel, built a church in honour of Mary the holy Mother of God, in the thirty-first year after the Lord's passion."

latin_text: Johannes Tinmuthensis, ex Glastoniensis monasterii libris, ita rem narrat: "Ex^r quo apostoli in regiones diversas erant divisi ad prædicandum verbum vitæ, sanctus Philippus apostolus regionem Franciæ cum suis discipulis sortitus est: de quibus misit in Britanniam duodecim (quorum primus erat Joseph ab Arimathia, qui et Dominum sepelivit) anno ab incarnatione Domini sexagesimo tertio, et ab assumptione sanctæ Mariæ quinto decimo : quibus duodecim hidæ ab Arvirago paganicis erroribus decepto concessæ erant. Qui ibidem Deo servientes, per Gabrielis archangeli admonitionem; ecclesiam in honore sanctæ Dei genetricis Mariæ construxerant. Cumque fidem Christi constanter prædicarent, rex barbarus cum gente sua tam nova audiens et inconsueta, omnino prædicationi eorum consentire renuebat, nec paternas traditiones commutare volebat: quia tamen de longe venerant, ad petitionem eorum quandam insulam sylvis paludibusque circumdatam ad inhabitandum concessit. Erat enim portio illa duodecim hidarum, et quandam capellam (ut præmittitur) ex virgis torquatis construxerunt anno post passionem Domini XXXI.” Hæc Johannes^s Tinmuthensis, in sanctilogio Britanniæ, et ejus exscriptor Johannes Capgravius in nova legenda Angliæ, sed prudenter præmisso hoc prologo. “ Quæ inferius digesta sunt, apud Glastoniam ex libris monasterii illius excerpsi: quæ si veritatem sapiant, lectoris arbitrio relinquo.” Et hoc ad extremum subjecto epilogo. “ Ego vero in præscriptis et dubiis, et in sequentibus nonnullis, authoritatem discutiendi et definiendi mihi non præsumo: sed tanquam relator simplex, quæ in diversis libris et locis cum laboribus et difficultate sedulus indagator reperire potui, ardua peritis ventilanda relinquens, sine invidia communico.”

translation_history.english: John of Tynemouth, drawing on the books of the monastery of Glastonbury, tells the story in this way: "After^r the apostles had been dispersed into different regions to preach the word of life, the holy apostle Philip received the region of France as his lot, together with his disciples; and from among them he sent twelve into Britain (of whom the first was Joseph of Arimathea, who also buried the Lord) in the sixty-third year from the incarnation of the Lord, and the fifteenth from the assumption of holy Mary. To these men twelve hides were granted by Arviragus, who was deceived by pagan errors. Serving God in that place, at the admonition of the archangel Gabriel they built a church in honour of Mary the holy Mother of God. And when they preached the faith of Christ steadfastly, the barbarian king, hearing along with his people things so new and unfamiliar, refused altogether to assent to their preaching, nor was he willing to change his ancestral traditions; yet because they had come from far away, at their petition he granted them for their dwelling a certain island surrounded by woods and marshes. For that holding was the portion of twelve hides, and they built a certain chapel (as stated above) of twisted withies, in the thirty-first year after the Lord's passion." So John^s of Tynemouth, in his "Sanctilogy of Britain", and his transcriber John Capgrave in the "New Legend of England" — though the latter prudently prefaces it with this prologue: "What is set out below I excerpted at Glastonbury from the books of that monastery; whether these things have the savour of truth I leave to the reader's judgement." And he appends at the end this epilogue: "For my part, in the matters set down above, both the doubtful ones and several that follow, I do not presume to myself the authority of examining and determining; but as a simple reporter I share without ill-will, leaving hard questions to be sifted by the learned, whatever I, a diligent investigator, have been able to find with labour and difficulty in various books and places."

latin_text: Polydorus Vergilius, vir naris emunctioris, sublatis crassioribus illis monachorum fabulamentis, historiam hanc ita proponit. “ Joseph^t ille, qui, teste Matthæo evangelista, ab Arimathæa civitate oriundus, Christi corpus sepeliverat, sive casu, sive consilio, ita volente Deo, cum non parvo comitatu, in Britanniam venit: ubi tam ipse, quam ejus socii, cum de evangelio prædicarent, atque dogma Christi sedulo docerent, multi per hæc ad veram pietatem traducti, salutiferaque fruge imbuti, baptizati sunt. Isti viri certe divino spiritu aﬄati, cum a rege parum terræ ad inhabitandum (proxime Welliam oppidum, circiter millia passuum quatuor) dono accepissent, ibi novæ religionis prima jecerunt fundamenta, ubi hodie est templum magnificum cœnobiumque monasticæ familiæ D. Benedicti ordinis nobile. Loco nomen est Glasconia. Hæc omnino Christianæ pietatis in Britannia extitere primordia; quam deinde Lucius rex, sicut paulo post dicemus, prope extinctam baptismi fonte sublatus mirabiliter accendit, pieque adauxit. Nam Gildas testis est, Britannos jam inde ab initio orti evangelii, Christianam recepisse religionem."

translation_history.english: Polydore Vergil, a man of keener discernment, sets the story out as follows, once those grosser monkish fables have been cleared away: "That Joseph^t who, on the testimony of Matthew the evangelist, was a native of the city of Arimathea and had buried the body of Christ, came into Britain with a considerable retinue, whether by chance or by design, God so willing; and there, when he and his companions preached the gospel and diligently taught the doctrine of Christ, many were by these means brought over to true piety and, imbued with its saving fruit, were baptized. These men, assuredly inspired by the divine Spirit, having received from the king as a gift a small piece of land to dwell on (close to the town of Wells, about four miles off), there laid the first foundations of the new religion, at the place where today there stands a magnificent church and a noble monastery of the monastic family of the order of St. Benedict. The place is named Glastonbury. These were altogether the first beginnings of Christian piety in Britain; and afterwards King Lucius, as I shall relate shortly, when that piety had almost died out, was himself raised up by the font of baptism and marvellously rekindled it and piously increased it. For Gildas testifies that the Britons received the Christian religion from the very beginning of the rise of the gospel."

Et extat sane adhuc magni nostri Patricii nomine, a Glastoniensibus monachis conficta epistola (charta ea est B. Patricii, a Malmesburiensi superius citata) in qua de origine ecclesiæ quæ Anglo-Saxonibus Ealdcirc, id est, vetusta ecclesia dicta est, ita ille disserens introducitur. “Ostenderunt mihi fratres scripta sanctorum Phagani et Deruviani: in quibus continebatur, quod duodecim discipuli sanctorum Philippi et Jacobi ipsam vetustam ecclesiam construxerant in honore prælibatæ advocatricis nostræ, B. Mariæ virginis, per doctrinamentum beati archangeli Gabrielis. Insuper et quod Dominus eandem ecclesiam cœlitus in honore suæ matris dedicaverat: et quod tres reges pagani ipsis duodecim, ad eorum sustenementum, duodecim portiones terræ dederunt.” Indeque Malmesburiensis: “ Duodecim discipulis sanctorum Philippi et Jacobi anno Dominicæ Incarnationis LXIII. in Britanniam venientibus, tres reges licet pagani XII. portiones terræ contulerunt: unde adhuc nomen XII. hidarum perseverat.” Hæc ille in libro de antiquitate Glastoniensis ecclesiæ: ubi XII. harum hidarum metas cum locis præcipuis quæ intra earum limites continentur, diligenter describit. Earundem etiam in libro censuali Guilielmi I. Anglorum regis, qui Domesday^y appellatur, ejusmodi fit mentio. “ Ecclesia Glastingebury habet in ipsa villa XII. hydas quæ nunquam geldaverunt.”

translation_history.english: Thomas Scrope, once bishop of Dromore in Ireland, reports the same things about Joseph's arrival in the seventh chapter of the book he wrote on the antiquity of the Carmelite order. So too does Thomas Harfeld, in his breviary of the kings of the English, where he says that Fagan and Duvian (or Deruvian), in the times of king Lucius, found in the isle of Avalon "an ancient church built by the disciples of Christ, together with ancient writings telling how, when the holy apostles were dispersed to preach, St Philip came into France and sent twelve of his disciples into Britain, setting Joseph of Arimathea over them." And there is indeed still extant, under the name of our great Patrick, a letter forged by the monks of Glastonbury (it is the charter of St Patrick cited above from William of Malmesbury), in which he is introduced discoursing on the origin of the church which the Anglo-Saxons called Ealdcirc, that is, the old church: "The brethren showed me the writings of Saints Phagan and Deruvian, in which it was set down that twelve disciples of Saints Philip and James had built that old church in honour of our aforementioned advocate, the Blessed Virgin Mary, by the instruction of the blessed archangel Gabriel; and further, that the Lord had himself dedicated that same church from heaven in honour of his mother; and that three pagan kings gave those twelve men twelve portions of land for their sustenance." And from this William of Malmesbury writes: "To the twelve disciples of Saints Philip and James, who came into Britain in the year of our Lord's Incarnation 63, three kings, pagan though they were, granted twelve portions of land, from which the name of the Twelve Hides survives to this day." So he says in his book on the antiquity of the church of Glastonbury, where he carefully describes the bounds of these twelve hides along with the principal places contained within their limits. The same hides are mentioned in like manner in the survey book of William I, king of the English, which is called Domesday^y: "The church of Glastingebury holds in that same vill twelve hides which have never paid geld."

translation_history.english: A hide is said to be as much land as suffices to support a household (hence what Bede in his Ecclesiastical History calls a familia, his Saxon translator renders Hẏdelandeꞃ), or as much as can be tilled in a year by a single plough; as our antiquaries^a observe both from Dunstan's charter granted in the year 963, in which he grants a piece of land "of seven ploughs^z, which in English is called seven hides," and from Matthew Paris, Henry of Huntingdon, John of London, Thomas Walsingham, and others. That those three kings — Arviragus, Marius, and Coilus — were pagans I find noted in the margin of the Malmesbury manuscript held in the library of Trinity College, Cambridge; and John Capgrave hints at the same, though he is hardly consistent with himself here. For in his Life of Patrick, following John of Tynemouth and Harding in his chronicle^b, he writes that those twelve hides were granted by Arviragus; but in his Life of Joseph, that they were granted by two of Arviragus's successors, Marius the son of Arviragus and Coilus the son of Marius. John Harding, however, scarcely allows that these kings were pagans, for he relates that Arviragus was converted to the faith by Joseph of Arimathea^c and washed in the baptism of salvation, and that Marius^d and Coilus were to some degree instructed in the Christian religion, although they did not attain the perfection that would have been fitting. In the same way Richard^e White of Basingstoke says that Arviragus was "well disposed toward the Christian religion," and that Coilus too, his grandson by his son Marius, was "somewhat instructed in the Christian religion during his lifetime, yet not so as to profess it publicly."

For so Gildas the Briton, a Christian writer who for his outstanding learning is surnamed the Wise, recorded nearly eleven hundred years ago; and all the annals of the English thereafter confirm it.”

Habet enim secum Joseph in sarcophago duo vascula alba et argentea, cruore prophetiæ Jesu et sudore perimpleta.

translation_history.english: These words of his are put forward, which I set out here as copied from various^k exemplars, although they are utterly unworthy of being read. “The island of Avalon, greedy for the burial of pagans, adorned beyond all others in the world for the sepulture of them all with the prophesying spherules of prophecy, and adorned for the time to come, will be most exalted for those who praise. Abbadare^l, mighty in Saphat^m, most noble of the pagans, received his sleep there together with one hundred and four thousand. Among these Joseph de Marmore^n (of Arimathea by name) took his perpetual sleep. And he lies in a forked line beside the southern corner of the oratory made ready^o with wattles, above the mighty Virgin who is to be adored, the aforesaid spherule-bearers having^p thirteen places. For Joseph has with him in his sarcophagus two vessels, white and of silver, filled full with the blood and sweat of the prophecy of Jesus.

latin_text: Cum reperietur ejus sarcophagum integrum, illibatum, in futuris temporibus videbitur; et erit apertum toto orbi terrarum. Et tunc nec aqua nec ros cœli insulam nobilissimam habitantibus poterit deficere. Per multum tempus ante diem judicialem in Josaphat erant aperta hæc et viventibus declarata.” Hunc Mevinum Britannum chronographum appellat Johannes Hardingus in chronico suo poemate^p, pro quo Nenii nomen, capite octavo et quadragesimo irrepsit : ubi bellam istam ex eo recitat fabellam, quod Josephus Arvirago regi pro gentis Britannicæ insignibus crucem, quæ Georgiana postea dicta est, in clypeo argenteo depictam tradiderit.

translation_history.english: When his sarcophagus is found whole and undefiled, it will be seen in times to come; and it will lie open to the whole world. And then neither water nor the dew of heaven will be able to fail those who inhabit that most noble island. For a long time before the day of judgement, in Josaphat, these things were open and declared to the living.” John Harding, in his chronicle in verse^p, calls this Mevinus a British chronographer — for which name that of Nennius has crept in, in chapter forty-eight — where he recites from him that pretty little tale, that Joseph handed over to Arviragus, king of the Britons, as the arms of the British nation, a cross, afterwards called St George's, painted on a silver shield.

latin_text: Et eo antiquior alius, ad marginem Matthæi Florilegi MS. in bibliotheca D. Jacobi Waræi, Melkinus (vel potius Mewynus) qui ante Merlinum fuit, inter cætera gesta de temporibus Britonum in libro suo hæc dicit; “Joseph ab Arimathia nobilis decurio in insula Avaloniæ cum XI. sociis suis somnum cepit perpetuum: et jacet in meridiano angulo lineæ bifurcatæ oratorii adorandæ virginis. For he has with him two white vessels of silver, filled full with the blood and sweat of the great prophet Jesus. And for a long time before the day of Judgement his body will be found whole and undefiled; and it will lie open to the whole world. Then neither dew nor rain will fail those who inhabit that most noble island.

latin_text: Verum et otio meo et lectoris patientia abutar, si nugacissima commenta, quæ ex stramentitiis ejusmodi scriptis tum ab Hardingo et Capgravio, tum in magna Glastoniensium tabula de Josepho referuntur, commemorem. Illud minime prætereundum, quod in Europæanorum nostrorum synodis generalibus, quando de Britannici regni dignitate cum Gallis et Hispanis habita est controversia, ad hanc de Josepho traditionem provocare subinde soliti sunt Anglicanæ gentis oratores. Agitata est hæc quæstio anno MCCCCIX. in Pisano primum, deinde anno MCCCCXVII. in Constantiensi concilio : ex quo excerpta est “ Nobilissima disceptatio super dignitate et magnitudine regnorum Britannici et Gallici, habita ab utriusque oratoribus et legatis in concilio Constantiensi,” Lovanii anno MDXVII. typis excusa. Eam ex actis concilii in ipsa urbe Constantiensi asservatis edendam curavit D. Robertus Wingfeldius eques auratus, Henrici VIII. Anglorum regis ad Maximilianum imperatorem orator : quam etiam in duobus MSS.^r ejusdem concilii exemplaribus invenimus. Hic vero quum in tricesima sessione mota est hæc quæstio : “ an juri et rationi consonum sit, æquiparare regnum Angliæ regno Franciæ, in concilio generali :” pro dignitate Ecclesiæ Anglicanæ, inter alia allegatum est, quod “ Statim^s post passionem Christi Joseph ab Arimathia, nobilis decurio, qui Christum de cruce deposuit, cum XII. sociis vineam Domini de mane colendam, Angliam videlicet ingressus est, et populos ad fidem convertit. Quibus rex XII. hidas terræ in diocesi Bathoniensi pro victu assignavit: qui in monasterio Glastoniensi Bathoniensis diocesis, ut scribitur, tumulantur. Super quibus XII. hidis prædictis dictum monasterium antiquitus dotatum dignoscitur. Sed regnum Franciæ tempore sancti Dionysii et ejus ministerio fidem Christi recepit.”

translation_history.english: But I would abuse both my own leisure and the reader's patience were I to rehearse the utterly trifling fictions concerning Joseph which are reported out of such strawy writings, whether by Harding and Capgrave or in the great Table of the Glastonbury monks. This much, however, must be set down: that in the general synods of our Europeans, whenever controversy arose with the French and the Spanish over the dignity of the British kingdom, the orators of the English nation were repeatedly in the habit of appealing to this tradition concerning Joseph. The question was agitated in the year 1409, first at the Council of Pisa, and then in the year 1417 at the Council of Constance; from the latter was excerpted the "Most Noble Disputation on the Dignity and Greatness of the British and French Kingdoms, Held by the Orators and Legates of Both in the Council of Constance," printed at Louvain in the year 1517. Sir Robert Wingfield, knight, ambassador of Henry VIII, king of the English, to the emperor Maximilian, saw to its publication from the acts of the council preserved in the city of Constance itself; and I have found it also in two manuscript^r copies of the same council. Here indeed, when in the thirtieth session this question was raised — "whether it is consonant with law and reason to equate the kingdom of England with the kingdom of France in a general council" — it was alleged, among other things, on behalf of the dignity of the English Church, that "Immediately^s after the passion of Christ, Joseph of Arimathea, the noble decurion who took Christ down from the cross, entered with twelve companions upon the Lord's vineyard to be cultivated from the morning — that is, he entered England — and converted its peoples to the faith. To these men the king assigned twelve hides of land in the diocese of Bath for their maintenance; and they are buried, as it is written, in the monastery of Glastonbury in the diocese of Bath. Upon these aforesaid twelve hides the said monastery is known to have been endowed in ancient times. But the kingdom of France received the faith of Christ in the time of Saint Denis and through his ministry."

latin_text: a Richardo Flemmingo Lincolniensi episcopo et Lincolniensis collegii apud Oxonienses conditore, propositum est: quum adversus Hispanos, Scotos et Gallos coram Martino V. ab Anglis renovata esset hæc controversia. Sed in Basileensi præcipue concilio, anno MCCCCXXXIV. inter oratores regis Angliæ et Castellæ efferbuit hæc contentio : ubi quæ nostris hac in parte ab Alphonso Garsia de sancta Maria, legum doctore ac Compostellanæ et Segobiensis ecclesiarum decano, objecta sunt, ex schedis Cottonianis visum est proponere, et excutere. “Oratores regis Angliæ,” ait ille, “tam in præsentia vestrarum reverendissimarum paternitatum, quam in sacra deputatione reformatorii, dixerunt præferendos se propter antiquiorem susceptionem fidei Christianæ. Nam dicunt, quod ille nobilis decurio Joseph ab Arimathia una cum aliis, anno XV. post assumptionem gloriosæ virginis Mariæ venit in Angliam, et magnam ejus partem ad fidem Christi convertit.

translation_history.english: and was put forward by Richard Flemming, bishop of Lincoln and founder of Lincoln College at Oxford, when this controversy had been revived by the English against the Spaniards, the Scots, and the French before Martin V. But it was chiefly in the Council of Basel, in the year 1434, that this dispute boiled up between the envoys of the king of England and those of the king of Castile; and I have thought it well to set out from the Cottonian papers, and to examine, the objections brought on this head against our countrymen by Alfonso Garsia de Santa Maria, doctor of laws and dean of the churches of Compostela and Segovia. “The envoys of the king of England,” he says, “both in the presence of your most reverend paternities and in the sacred deputation for reform, have declared that they ought to be given precedence on account of their earlier reception of the Christian faith. For they say that that noble decurion Joseph of Arimathea, together with others, came into England in the fifteenth year after the assumption of the glorious Virgin Mary, and converted a great part of it to the faith of Christ.

latin_text: Et post non longo tempore a passione Christi, Eleutherius papa regnum Angliæ totaliter convertit ad fidem.”

translation_history.english: And not long after the passion of Christ, Pope Eleutherius converted the kingdom of England wholly to the faith.”

latin_text: Ad primum vero illud de Josepho respondet. I. “Per interemptionem. Nego enim (inquit) Joseph illum venisse in Angliam. Ille ergo qui dicit, probat: (juxta l. Ei qui ff. de proba.) Producatur ergo in medium aliqua historia vel scriptura authentica. II. Per probabilitatem contrariam. Nam licet ei qui negat non incumbat probatio: (ut l. actor. C. de proba.) tamen interdum probatur negativa per judicium; quando habet comitantiam temporum. (ut l. optimam C. contrahentium et com. stipu.)

translation_history.english: To that first argument concerning Joseph he replies as follows. I. “By outright denial. For I deny (he says) that that Joseph came into England. He therefore who makes the assertion must prove it (according to the law Ei qui, Digest, On Proofs). Let some authentic history or written document, then, be produced. II. By contrary probability. For although the burden of proof does not rest upon the one who denies (as in the law Actor, Code, On Proofs), yet a negative is sometimes established by inference, when it has a concurrence of dates in its favour (as in the law Optimam, Code, On Contracting and Entering into Stipulations).

latin_text: In hoc ergo casu bene potest probari hæc negativa per scripturam contrariam. Continetur enim in floribus sanctorum, sub legenda Jacobi minoris, contrarium. Hoc legitur quoque quod Titus intrans Hierusalem, quemdam murum densissimum vidit, ipsumque perforari jussit: et intus quendam senem repererunt, qui dixit se esse Joseph ab Arimathia, et se ibidem esse inclusum a Judæis quia Christum sepelisset, et quod usque ad tempus istud cœlesti cibo sit pastus. In evangelio tamen Nicodemi dicitur^t, quod Christus eum liberavit post resurrectionem suam, et in Arimathiam duxit. Potest autem dici quod eductus cum a prædicatione non cessaret, iterum sit ab ipsis Judæis inclusus. Hæc ubi supra. Cum ergo Joseph fuerit incarceratus tanto tempore apud Jerusalem, impossibile est eum fuisse in Anglia, cum sit magna distantia.

translation_history.english: In this case, then, this negative can well be proved from a written testimony to the contrary. For the contrary is contained in the “Flowers of the Saints,” under the legend of James the Less. There it is also read that Titus, on entering Jerusalem, saw a certain very thick wall and ordered it to be broken through; and inside they found an old man who said that he was Joseph of Arimathea, and that he had been shut up there by the Jews because he had buried Christ, and that up to that time he had been fed with heavenly food. In the Gospel of Nicodemus, however, it is said^t that Christ set him free after his resurrection and brought him to Arimathea. But it may be said that, once released, since he did not cease from preaching, he was shut up again by those same Jews. So far the passage cited above. Since, then, Joseph was imprisoned for so long a time at Jerusalem, it is impossible that he was in England, given the great distance.

latin_text: III. Potest dici, quod licet hoc fuisset verum, (quod tamen non fuit) non sequitur ergo quod totum solium illud suscepit fidem. IV. Dicitur, dato illo quod negatur, adhuc tamen Hispani primo susceperunt fidem, quod probatur, quia Jacobus martyrium subiit vivente Petro. Scriptum est enin de Herode, quod occidit Jacobum gladio, et apposuit ut apprehenderet Petrum, Actuum capite duodecimo. Sed constat, quod Petrus passus est sub Nerone.

translation_history.english: III. It may be said that, even if this had been true (which in fact it was not), it does not therefore follow that that whole realm received the faith. IV. It is said that, even granting what is denied, the Spaniards still received the faith first; and this is proved because James suffered martyrdom while Peter was still alive. For it is written of Herod that he killed James with the sword and proceeded to seize Peter as well (Acts 12). But it is agreed that Peter suffered under Nero.

latin_text: Nero autem fuit prope annum Domini LIV. et Titus fuit prope annum Domini LXXX. Jam certum est quod si Joseph fuisset in Anglia, hoo fuisset postquam de carcere fuisset liberatus per Titum, et sic post octogesimum annum a nativitate Domini: et Jacobus mortuus est ante Neronem pluribus annis, quasi prope quadragesimum annum a nativitate Domini. Et Hispania suscepit fidem a Jaoobo, vivente eo, vel statim in sepultura ejus; ut supra dixi. Ergo Hispania est in fide antiquior." Hæc ad patres Basileensis concilii Alphonsus Garsias: in quibus quædam sunt levia admodum, nonnulla etiam oppido ridicula.

translation_history.english: Now Nero was about the year of the Lord 54, and Titus about the year of the Lord 80. It is therefore certain that, if Joseph was in England, this must have been after he had been freed from prison by Titus, and thus after the eightieth year from the Lord's nativity; whereas James died many years before Nero, about the fortieth year from the Lord's nativity. And Spain received the faith from James while he was still alive, or immediately upon his burial, as I said above. Therefore Spain is the more ancient in the faith." Such were the arguments Alfonso Garsias laid before the fathers of the Council of Basel: among them some are exceedingly trivial, and several downright ridiculous.

latin_text: Ad primam ejus responsionem quod attinet: historias et scripta antiqua Josephi ad Britannos legationem confirmantia, quanta potuimus diligentia superius collegimus, atque in medium produximus. Quibus jam addimus oratorum et legatorum regis Angliæ, in hac ipsa synodo propositam assertionem. "Certum est in Anglia reperiri in libris antiquissimis et archivis, præcipue in archivis abbatiæ notabilis Glastonensis, diocesis Bathoniensis; quod Joseph ab Arimathia cum duodecim sociis, aut ex persecutione Herodiana, vel præsidum Romanorum in Judæa, ad Angliam vectus est. Ibidem, quæ de Christo viderat et audierat prædicavit, et prædicando plures convertit; convertendo, multa et infinita sibi, ab illis quos converterat ad fidem collata, conquæsivit; conquæsita postea templo Christo per eum erecto reliquit: (et hoc, tempore quo Petrus in Antiochia prædicavit fidem:) quod templum a Joseph erectum, in locum religiosum et abbatialem dignitatem translatum est, et laus Christi per notabile monasterium præservatur ad præsens."

translation_history.english: As for his first answer: I have collected above, with all the diligence I could, the ancient histories and writings that confirm Joseph's mission to the Britons, and have brought them forward for examination. To these I now add the assertion put forward in this very synod by the orators and ambassadors of the king of England: "It is certain that in England there is found, in the most ancient books and archives — especially in the archives of the notable abbey of Glastonbury, in the diocese of Bath — that Joseph of Arimathea, with twelve companions, was carried over to England, either from the Herodian persecution or from that of the Roman governors in Judaea. There he preached what he had seen and heard concerning Christ, and by his preaching converted many; by converting them he acquired many and countless possessions conferred upon him by those whom he had converted to the faith; and what he had acquired he afterwards left to the church he had erected to Christ (and this at the time when Peter was preaching the faith at Antioch). That church, erected by Joseph, was afterwards transformed into a religious house and raised to the dignity of an abbey, and the praise of Christ is preserved there to the present day by a notable monastery."

latin_text: Sive gestis Pilati apud Gregor. Turonens. histor. lib. 1. cap. 20.

translation_history.english: ^t Or in the Acts of Pilate, as given in Gregory of Tours, History, book 1, chapter 20.

latin_text: Probabilitatem contrariam, quam secundo loco urget, negamus omnino esse probabilem. Neque enim aliquem hodie, si Thomam Dempsterum exceperis^u, tam stulte credulum esse existimamus, cui absurdissimum illud commentum, de Josepho muro incluso, probabile videri possit: et de legendæ aureæ authore Jacobo de Voragine, ex^w cujus areolis fœtidi isti sanctorum flores sunt decerpti, in ipsa Hispania a Ludovico Vive^x et Melchiore Cano^y jamdudum lata est sententia; ferrei oris eum virum fuisse, atque plumbei cordis.

translation_history.english: The contrary probability which he urges in the second place I deny to be probable at all. For I do not suppose that anyone today—unless you make an exception of Thomas Dempster^u—is so foolishly credulous that that most absurd fabrication about Joseph walled up in a tomb could seem probable to him; and upon James of Voragine, the author of the "Golden Legend," from^w whose garden-plots those rank flowers of the saints have been plucked, sentence was long ago passed in Spain itself by Juan Luis Vives^x and Melchior Cano^y: that he was a man of iron mouth and leaden heart.

latin_text: Tertium illud, quod totum Britanniæ regnum Josephi ministerio fidem non susceperit; verum quidem est, sed ad rem non pertinet. Nam nec totum regnum Hispaniæ a Jacobo conversum fuisse ipsi Hispani dicent; nec integra regna ab ullo apostolorum Christiana facta esse constat: et de antiquitate, non de universalitate susceptionis fidei instituta est quæstio.

translation_history.english: His third point—that the whole kingdom of Britain did not receive the faith through Joseph's ministry—is indeed true, but beside the question. For not even the Spaniards themselves will say that the whole kingdom of Spain was converted by James; nor is it established that entire kingdoms were made Christian by any of the apostles: and the question raised concerns the antiquity, not the universality, of the reception of the faith.

latin_text: Quartum vero et postremum, partim incertis, partim falsis nititur fundamentis. Jacobi prædicationem in Hispania, inter incerta posuit Rodericus Ximenius Toletanus archiepiscopus, in concertatione quam anno MCCXV. in Lateranensi concilio cum præsule Compostellano de primatu habuit. Ejus verba, a Garsia Loaisa e libro MS. bibliothecæ Toletanæ edita, hæc sunt. “ Si^z inducat (Compostellanus) primam divini verbi promulgationem, et plurimorum conversionem ad fidem Christi in Hispania (per Jacobum factam:) qui divinam paginam noverunt, testimonium perhibeant. Ego tantum legi, datam ei fuisse potestatem prædicandi in Hispania: sed interim, cum per Judæam et Samariam divinam legem seminaret, sub Herode Hierosolymis truncato capite exhalavit animam, et Domino reddidit. Quomodo ergo ibi prædicavit, quo nondum ingressus est? aut sine prædicatione, quos, obsecro, convertit ad Dominum?” Nec ex parte altera certum est, quantumvis id ita esse affirmet Alphonsus, “ quod si Joseph fuisset in Anglia, hoc fuisset postquam de carcere liberatus fuisset per Titum, et sic post octuagesimum annum a nativitate Domini.” A Tito enim, anno æræ Christianæ (non octogesimo sed) septuagesimo eversam esse Hierosolymam certum est: quæ vero de Josepho Arimathæensi tunc per eum liberato pro certis assumuntur, nugæ sunt nugerrimæ.

translation_history.english: The fourth and last point rests on foundations partly uncertain, partly false. Rodrigo Ximénez, archbishop of Toledo, placed James's preaching in Spain among things uncertain, in the contest which he held in the year 1215 at the Lateran Council with the bishop of Compostela concerning the primacy. His words, published by García de Loaisa from a manuscript of the library of Toledo, are these: "If he (the bishop of Compostela)^z should allege the first promulgation of the divine word, and the conversion of very many to the faith of Christ in Spain (as accomplished by James), let those who know the sacred page bear witness. I have read only that power was given him to preach in Spain; but in the meantime, while he was sowing the divine law throughout Judaea and Samaria, he was beheaded under Herod at Jerusalem, breathed out his soul, and rendered it to the Lord. How then did he preach in a place he had never entered? Or without preaching, whom, I ask, did he convert to the Lord?" Nor is it certain on the other side, however firmly Alphonsus affirms it, "that if Joseph had been in England, this must have been after he had been freed from prison by Titus, and so after the eightieth year from the birth of the Lord." For it is certain that Jerusalem was overthrown by Titus in the (not eightieth but) seventieth year of the Christian era; and the things taken for certain about Joseph of Arimathea's being then freed by him are the emptiest of trifles.

latin_text: Apparat. ad histor. Scot. lib. 1. cap. 7. pag. 27. Vid. Melchiorem Inchofer, de veritate epistolæ B. Mariæ ad Messanenses, cap. 13. pag. 71, 72.

latin_text: Guilielmus^a quidem Eysengreineus ex annalibus Anglorum narrat eum “ post urbis Hierosolymæ destructionem apostolis adhæsisse; atque hoc pacto jam senem in Britanniam profectum, in urbe Wellia Christum prædicavisse.” Sed temporis illam circumstantiam in nullis Anglorum annalibus expressam reperit. Glastonienses, et Malmesburiensis monachus in secundo Eulogii sui libro, Josephi adventum ad annum Christi LXIII. referunt: quem ab assumptione beatæ virginis XV. fuisse tradunt.

translation_history.english: Wilhelm^a Eysengrein, indeed, relates on the authority of the English annals that he “attached himself to the apostles after the destruction of the city of Jerusalem, and that in this way, already an old man, he set out for Britain and preached Christ in the city of Wells.” But he finds that chronological detail stated in none of the English annals. The Glastonbury writers, and the monk of Malmesbury in the second book of his “Eulogium,” assign Joseph’s arrival to the year of Christ 63, which they record to have been the fifteenth from the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin.

latin_text: Oratores Angli, ut diximus, in Basileensi hoc concilio, templum a Josepho in Britannia erectum asserunt, “ tempore quo Petrus in Antiochia prædicavit fidem :” et in Constantiensi, “ statim post passionem Christi” eundem Britanniam ingressum esse, et populos ad fidem convertisse defendunt. Quod et cum ipsius Josephi ætate, qui Domino passionem adeunte inter Judæos senator^b honoratus fuerat, et cum iis quæ initio ex Gilda de tempore summo Tiberii Cæsaris produximus, bene quadrat.

translation_history.english: The English envoys, as I have said, assert at this Council of Basel that the church was erected by Joseph in Britain “at the time when Peter preached the faith at Antioch”; and at Constance they maintain that the same man entered Britain “immediately after the Passion of Christ” and converted the peoples to the faith. This agrees well both with the age of Joseph himself, who at the time the Lord went to his Passion had been an honoured councillor^b among the Jews, and with what I adduced at the outset from Gildas concerning the closing period of Tiberius Caesar.

latin_text: Collect. Concil. Hispan. a Loaisa edit. pag. 291. et Concil. edit. Colon. an. 1618. tom. 2. part. 2. pag. 317, 318. Vide Baron. annal. tom. 9. an. 816. sec. 49, 50, 51, 52. et bibliothec. Floriacens. Joannis a Bosco, part. 2. pag. 184.

latin_text: Johannes enim Hardingius indignus est, cujus hic ulla habeatur ratio : qui^c Josephum per ipsos quadraginta duos a Christi morte annos, non quidem in muro, sed in Caiphæ carcere detentum, sine omni cibo et potu vixisse ; deinde a Vespasiano liberatum, et in Britanniam anno Christi LXXVI. perductum, ibique regi Arvirago et conjugi ipsius Genissæ (quæ Claudii imperatoris filia fuisse fingitur) commendatum fuisse fabulatur. Johannes Balæus, Ossoriensis aliquando apud Hibernos episcopus, eodem illo anno ex vita hac migrasse eum scribit. “ In sancta senectute (inquit^d) Josephus inter discipulos tandem quietam morte carnis dormitionem accepit, in Avalonica solitudine sepultus, anno a Christi incarnatione LXXVI. Mario regnante in Britannia. Postea translatum est ejus corpus ad Glasconiense monachorum collegium, et in pretiosa theca repositum. Neque desunt (inquit ille) qui ex conjecturis habeant, contexuisse illum ad ecclesias Britannorum epistolas quasdam.” Quam conjecturam ut verisimiliorem redderet Guilielmus Eysengreineus, ne a præsente ad præsentes literæ scriptæ putarentur, “ reliquisse insulam et, ut renovaret sui memoriam, scripsisse epistolam ad Britannos” illum fingit: Anglorum hic quoque citatis annalibus ; in quibus tamen neque Britanniam eum reliquisse, neque ejusmodi aliquam epistolam scripsisse, neque alibi quam Glastoniæ mortuum et sepultum fuisse, uspiam traditum invenimus^e.

translation_history.english: For John Harding deserves no consideration here: he^c tells the tale that Joseph, throughout the whole forty-two years from the death of Christ, was held not indeed within a wall but in the prison of Caiaphas, and lived without any food or drink at all; then that he was set free by Vespasian and brought into Britain in the year of Christ 76, and there commended to king Arviragus and to his wife Genissa (who is fictitiously made out to have been the daughter of the emperor Claudius). John Bale, at one time bishop of Ossory among the Irish, writes that he departed this life in that same year. “In holy old age (he says^d) Joseph at last received among the disciples a quiet falling asleep by the death of the flesh, and was buried in the solitude of Avalon, in the year 76 from the incarnation of Christ, while Marius was reigning in Britain. Afterwards his body was translated to the college of monks at Glastonbury and laid up in a precious shrine. Nor are there lacking (he says) those who hold, on conjecture, that he composed certain epistles to the churches of the Britons.” To make this conjecture more plausible, Wilhelm Eysengrein — so that the letters might not be thought written by one present to those present — invents that he “left the island and, in order to renew the memory of himself, wrote an epistle to the Britons”: here too citing the annals of the English; in which, however, I find it nowhere recorded either that he left Britain, or that he wrote any epistle of the kind, or that he died and was buried anywhere but at Glastonbury^e.

latin_text: Mar. cap. 15. ver. 43. εὐσχήμων βουλευτής· quod a vulgato interprete, nobilis decurio, redditur, de quo videndus commentarius B. Hieronymi in Matth. cap. 27. et Ludovici de Dieu V. Grotius on Matt. 27:57. Those who in Pliny the Younger, book 10, letter 113, are called Buleutae are, in Trajan's rescript, letter 114, called decuriones.

translation_history.english: ^c John Harding, “Chronicle,” chapter 47.

translation_history.english: ^d Bale, “The Writers of Britain,” century 1, chapter 22.

latin_text: Extat vetustus catalogus sanctorum in Anglia sepultorum Saxonice scriptus, ac Latine, a Gotcelino Bertiniano monacho Cantuariensi, Anselmi archiepiscopi diebus editus: et de reliquis in Glastoniensi monasterio repositis libellus alter, Henrici III. Anglorum regis temporibus exaratus. In neutro vero Josephi ulla occurrit mentio.

translation_history.english: There exists an ancient catalogue of the saints buried in England, written in Saxon and in Latin, published by Gotcelinus of Bertin, a monk of Canterbury, in the days of Archbishop Anselm; and there is another small book on the relics deposited in the monastery of Glastonbury, drawn up in the time of Henry III, king of the English. But in neither does any mention of Joseph occur.

latin_text: Anno demum MCCCXLV. a Johanne Blomæo Londinensi, cujusdam revelationis sibi factæ prætextu, ab Edvardo III. licentia quærendi corpus Josephi ab Arimathia impetrata est: quam, ex archivis regiis^f in arce Londinensi asservatis a me descriptam, lectori communicare non gravabor.

translation_history.english: At length, in the year 1345, a licence to search for the body of Joseph of Arimathea was obtained from Edward III by John Blome of London, on the pretext of a revelation made to him; and since I have transcribed it myself from the royal archives^f kept in the Tower of London, I will readily share it with the reader.

latin_text: “Rex omnibus ad quos, &c. salutem. Supplicavit nobis Johannes Blome de London, ut cum sibi (sicut asserit) divinitus sit injunctum, ut venerandum corpus decurionis nobilis Josephi ab Arimathia, quod infra septa monasterii Glastoniensis in Christo quiescit humatum, et est ad honorem et multorum ædificationem his temporibus revelandum, quærat donec inveniat diligenter. Et quia in quibusdam antiquis scripturis dicitur contineri corpus ejus ibidem fuisse sepultum. Nos, si sit ita, desiderantes monumentum ejus, et venerandas ipsius reliquias, qui redemptori nostro morienti tantum exhibebat pietatis et humanitatis obsequium, corpus ejus de cruce deponendo, et illud in monumento suo novo ponendo, devotis honoribus prævenire; et sperantes nobis et toti regno nostro ex revelatione prædicta gratiam uberiorem provenire: concessimus et licentiam dedimus (quantum in nobis est) eidem Johanni quod ipse infra præcinctum dicti monasterii fodere, et illas prætiosas reliquias juxta injunctionem et revelationem sibi factam quærere valeat in locis ubi melius viderit expedire: dum tamen absque damno dilectorum nobis in Christo, abbatis et conventus dicti monasterii, et ruina ecclesiæ et domorum suarum ibidem id fieri valeat; et quod ad id ipsorum abbatis et conventus licentiam habeat et assensum. In cujus, &c. Teste Rege PER IPSUM REGEM.

translation_history.english: “The King to all to whom, etc., greeting. John Blome of London has petitioned us that, since it has been divinely enjoined upon him (as he asserts) that he should diligently seek, until he find it, the venerable body of the noble decurion Joseph of Arimathea, which rests buried in Christ within the precincts of the monastery of Glastonbury and is in these times to be revealed to the honour and the edification of many; and because it is said to be contained in certain ancient writings that his body was buried in that same place: we therefore, if this be so, desiring to honour with devout observance his tomb and his venerable relics — the relics of one who showed to our dying Redeemer so great a service of piety and humanity, in taking down his body from the cross and laying it in his own new tomb — and hoping that from the aforesaid revelation a more abundant grace may come to us and to our whole kingdom, have granted and given licence (so far as it lies in us) to the same John, that he may dig within the precinct of the said monastery and search for those precious relics, in accordance with the injunction and revelation made to him, in whatever places he shall judge most expedient; provided always that this may be done without damage to our beloved in Christ, the abbot and convent of the said monastery, and without ruin to their church and houses there, and that for this he have the licence and assent of the abbot and convent themselves. In witness of which, etc. Witness the King. BY THE KING HIMSELF.

latin_text: Septoniæ enim sepultum fuisse (ea Dorsettensium Sćhaſtesburia est) per errorem scriptum legitur in Jo. Caii historiæ Cantabrig. lib. 1. pag. 23. nam Glasconiæ ibidem, pag. 31. legitur.

translation_history.english: ^e For it is by an error that he is said in writing to have been buried at Septonia (this is Shaftesbury in Dorset), in John Caius, History of Cambridge, book 1, p. 23; for in the same work, at p. 31, Glastonbury is what is read.
