translation_history.english: ^f Patent Rolls, 19 Edward III, part 1, membrane 8.

latin_text: Apud Westmonaster.

translation_history.english: At Westminster.

latin_text: VIII. die Junii.

translation_history.english: On the eighth day of June.

latin_text: Quem habuerit eventum ista inquisitio, non invenio: ab his tamen qui Glastoniense monasterium viderunt est proditum, et sacellum ibi Josephi nomini dicatum, et tumulum etiam positum fuisse, hoc inscriptum epitaphio.

translation_history.english: What outcome that inquiry had I do not find; yet it has been reported by those who saw the monastery of Glastonbury that a chapel there was dedicated to the name of Joseph, and that a tomb was also set up, inscribed with this epitaph.

latin_text: Ad Britones veni, postquam Christum sepelivi; -----------------------------------------docui, requievi.

translation_history.english: I came to the Britons after I had buried Christ; ----------------------------------------- I taught, I rested.

latin_text: Quibus adde, si libet, et Guilielmi Goodi Jesuitæ narrationem, qui Henrico VIII. regnante Glastoniæ natus et puer educatus est. " Glasconiæ^g extabant (inquit) laminæ æneæ sculptæ ad perpetuandam memoriam, sacella, crypta, cruces, arma, observatio festi S. Josephi ad VI. Calendas Augusti, quamdiu monachi regum chartis munitissime gaudebant: nunc omnia cum ruinis confusa perierunt.

translation_history.english: To these add, if you wish, the account of the Jesuit William Good, who was born at Glastonbury and brought up there as a boy in the reign of Henry VIII: "At Glastonbury^g there survived," he says, "engraved brass plates to perpetuate the memory, chapels, a crypt, crosses, arms, and the observance of the feast of St. Joseph on the sixth day before the Kalends of August, for as long as the monks enjoyed the fullest protection of the kings' charters; now everything has perished, lost amid the ruins.

latin_text: Nemo tamen monachorum unquam scivit certum locum sepulchri hujus sancti, vel designavit. Reconditum abditissime dixerunt, vel ibi, vel in monte, qui monti acuto vicinus, et cui nomen Hamden-hill : et futurum, ut quando reperietur corpus ejus, universus eo mundus confluat præ magnitudine et numero miraculorum quæ fient."

translation_history.english: Yet none of the monks ever knew the exact place of this saint's burial, or pointed it out. They said that it was hidden away in the deepest secrecy, either there or on the hill which lies next to the sharp hill and is called Hamden-hill; and that, when his body is found, the whole world will flock there because of the greatness and number of the miracles that will be worked."

latin_text: " Et inter cætera memini me vidisse Glasconiæ in cruce lapidea, quæ sub regina Elizabetha subversa fuit, laminam æneam in qua scribebatur, Josephum ab Arimathæa trigesimo anno post passionem Christi venisse in Britanniam cum undecim vel duodecim sociis, permissumque ei ab Arvirago rege, Glasconiæ quæ tunc erat insula dicta Avalonia, habitare, tanquam solitarios viros et simplices : et quod attulerit secum duo vasa argentea non grandia, in^h quibus erat de sanguine et aqua sacratissima, quæ profluxerat de latere Christi mortui. Crux autem ista erecta est ante multos annos ad denotandam longitudinem sacelli ab eodem sancto Josepho ex vimineis cratibus constructi in honorem beatissimæ virginis; deducta scilicet linea recta a medio illius crucis ad latus sacelli postea lapidibus quadratis exædificati: sub qua item erat olim illud sacellum Sancti Josephi in crypta subterranea. Foris autem in muro hujus sacelli beatæ virginis erant in lapide sculpta vetustissimis literis hæc duo verba, Jesus, Maria. Et confirmant antiqua arma Glasconiensis monasterii, quæ sunt hujusmodi: Scutum album in quo per longum erigitur stipes crucis viridis et nodosæ, et de latere ad latus extenduntur brachia seu rami crucis stipiti consimilia.

translation_history.english: "And among other things I remember that I saw at Glastonbury, on a stone cross which was pulled down in the reign of Queen Elizabeth, a brass plate on which was written that Joseph of Arimathea came into Britain in the thirtieth year after the passion of Christ with eleven or twelve companions, and that he was permitted by King Arviragus to live at Glastonbury — then an island called Avalonia — as men leading a solitary and simple life; and that he brought with him two small silver vessels, in^h which was some of the most sacred blood and water that had flowed from the side of the dead Christ. That cross was erected many years ago to mark the length of the chapel built by the same St. Joseph out of wattled wicker in honour of the most blessed Virgin, a straight line being drawn from the middle of that cross to the side of the chapel, which was afterwards built up in squared stone; and beneath it there was likewise once that chapel of St. Joseph in a subterranean crypt. Outside, on the wall of this chapel of the Blessed Virgin, these two words were carved in the stone in very ancient letters: Jesus, Maria. The ancient arms of the monastery of Glastonbury confirm this, and they are of this kind: a white shield on which the trunk of a green and knotted cross is raised lengthwise, and from side to side extend the arms, or branches, of the cross, matching the trunk.

latin_text: Edvard. Maihew congregat. Anglican. ordinis Benedict. Tabul. 2. pag. 1118, 1119.

translation_history.english: ^g Edward Maihew, of the English Congregation of the Benedictine Order, table 2, pp. 1118–1119.

latin_text: Sparguntur guttæ sanguinis per omnem aream scuti.

translation_history.english: Drops of blood are scattered over the whole field of the shield.

latin_text: Utrinque ad latera stipitis, et sub alis crucis, ponitur ampulla inaurata. Et hæc semper denominabantur insignia Sancti Josephi: qui ibi habitasse pie credebatur, et fortasse sepultus esse.”

translation_history.english: On either side, along the sides of the staff and beneath the arms of the cross, a gilded ampulla is set. And these were always called the arms of Saint Joseph, who was piously believed to have lived there, and perhaps to have been buried there.”

latin_text: Eundem cum sociis ibi fuisse sepultum, in magna Glastoniensium tabula ita traditum invenio. “ Ibi requiescunt XII. discipuli: quorum primas et custos fuit Joseph ab Arimathia, qui Dominum sepelivit. Multi ex paganis per eos ad fidem Christi conversi ac baptizati ibidem requiescunt, quorum, propter eorum multitudinem, non est numerus.” De iisdem eulogii author, libro secundo: “ Ibidem diu commorantes, multisque de dicto regno ad locum confluentibus per eosdem ad Christum conversis, tandem in pace quieverunt. Joseph vero ab Arimathia ibidem sepultus est juxta dictam Ecclesiam [B. Mariæ] cum duabus phialis plenis de sudore Christi sanguineo, quas secum de terra sancta detulerat.” Quis vero inde usque ad Lucii regis tempora loci illius status fuerit, Guilielmus Malmesburienſis his verbis edocet. “Sancti^i igitur memorati in eadem eremo sic degentes, eﬄuentibus multis annorum curriculis carnis ergastulo sunt educti: idemque locus cœpit esse ferarum latibulum, qui prius fuerat habitatio sanctorum.”

translation_history.english: That he was buried there together with his companions I find recorded, in the great tablet of Glastonbury, in these terms: “There rest twelve disciples, whose chief and guardian was Joseph of Arimathea, who buried the Lord. Many of the pagans converted by them to the faith of Christ and baptized rest in the same place, and, because of their multitude, they are without number.” Of the same men the author of the Eulogium writes, in book 2: “Remaining there for a long time, and many from the said kingdom flocking to the place and being converted to Christ through them, they at last rested in peace. Joseph of Arimathea indeed was buried there beside the said church [of the Blessed Mary], with two vials filled with the bloody sweat of Christ, which he had brought with him from the Holy Land.” But what the condition of that place was from then until the time of King Lucius, William of Malmesbury sets out in these words: “The saints^i already mentioned, then, living in this manner in that same hermitage, were, after the passage of many years, led out of the prison-house of the flesh; and the same place which had before been the dwelling of saints began to be the lair of wild beasts.”

latin_text: Vid. supr. pag. 31, et 37.

translation_history.english: ^h See above, pp. 31 and 37.

latin_text: Guil. Malmesbur. de antiquitat. Glaston. et eum secutus Johannes de Tinmouth, et Capgravius in vita Patricii.

translation_history.english: William of Malmesbury, "On the Antiquities of Glastonbury"; and, following him, John of Tynemouth, and Capgrave, in the "Life of Patrick."
